items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the tax law, in relation to facilitating the compliance of room remarketers with their obligation to collect sales tax on their sales of occupancy
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5732

TITLE OF BILL:
An act
to amend the tax law, in relation to facilitating the
compliance of room remarketers
with their obligation to collect sales tax on their sales of occupancy

PURPOSE:
The purpose of this legislation is to facilitate the compliance of
room remarketers with the duty to collect sales tax and New York City
hotel room occupancy tax on hotel occupancies.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:
Sections 1 and 2 of this bill adds new subdivision (r) to section
1111 of the Tax Law and the accompanying reference change, which would
provide the following relief to room remarketers. First, with regard
to transactions in which a customer obtains occupancy together with
other items, for one price, this bill provides room remarketers with
a way of computing the portion of the bill taxable as rent; the room
remarketers may compute such amount based on the consideration
payable to the hotel for the occupancy relative to the consideration
payable for the other items, or may use any other method authorized
by the commissioner Second, the bill would permit room remarketers to
not specify the amount of the sales tax due on occupancy at the time
the customer makes the reservation and instead to provide the
information on any invoice given to the customer prior to the
completion of the occupancy. Third, room remarketers would report
occupancy transactions in the sales tax filing period in which the
occupancy ended, rather than in the sales tax period during which
they collected the consideration for the occupancy. Fourth, section 3
of this bill amends Tax Law section 1119(e) to relieve a room
remarketer of the burden of obtaining the
certificate of authority number of the hotel that sold the occupancy
in order to qualify for a credit or refund of the sales tax the room
remarketer paid to the hotel for the occupancy.

Section 3 allows room remarketers to supply certain identifying
information about the hotel, including its address and telephone
number, instead of the certificate of authority number when the hotel
refuses to supply the latter number.

Sections 4-6 of the bill amends the New York City Administrative Code
to make some similar changes to provisions regarding room
remarketers' obligation to collect the City's hotel room occupancy
tax and to change some internal cross-references to other sections of
the Administrative Code.

EXISTING LAW:
Sales tax must generally be reported in the filing period in which the
seller collected the receipts from the sale (Tax Law § 1137[a)).
The seller must separately state the sales tax on any bill, invoice
or other memorandum of sale given to the customer (Tax Law §1132
[a][1]). Finally, if a room remarketer transaction involves a sale
of occupancy together with other items that are not taxable, the
charge for the whole bundle is taxable as rent unless the room


remarketer separately states on any invoice given to the customer a
charge for rent that is reasonable in relation to the value of the
other components of the bundle (Tax Law § 1105[e][2)).

JUSTIFICATION:
Last year's budget bill (section 4 of part AA of Chapter 57 of the
Laws of 2010) required room remarketers to collect sales tax on
sales of occupancy, and required room remarketers to collect New York
City hotel room occupancy taxes, while granting them a credit for
sales tax they paid to the hotels where the occupancy took place.
This bill makes a number of changes in the Tax Law and to the New
York City Administrative Code to better conform procedures to the
manner in which room remarketers have traditionally done business,
thereby lessening the compliance burden on them.

First, this bill revises the rule in last year's legislation regarding
sales in which a room remarketer bundles occupancy with nontaxable
items, such as airfare. Under last year's bill, the room remarketer
had to separately state the occupancy portion of the price of the
bundle ("bundled price") or treat the full amount of the bundled
price as rent and collect tax on that amount. The traditional
practice in the industry, however, is not to separately state the
price of the occupancy portion of the bundle on the invoice given the
customer. This bill conforms the sales tax and New York occupancy tax
to this industry practice by allowing a room remarketer to calculate
the portion of the bill taxable as rent based on the consideration
payable to the hotel for the occupancy relative to the consideration
payable for the other items.

The bill also allows the room remarketers to calculate the portion of
the bill taxable as rent based on any other method authorized by the
commissioner. With respect to New York City hotel occupancy tax, the
bill provides that the room remarketer may calculate the portion of
the bill taxable as rent based on the formula outlined above or,
alternatively, use any other reasonable method pursuant to which the
rent portion of the consideration would be no less than the
computation of rent under the formula.

Under last year's legislation, room remarketers are subject to the
usual sales tax rule that requires sales tax to be separately stated
on any invoice given the customer. The websites of most room
remarketers, however, are not set up to separate the state and local
sales tax from other taxes due on the occupancy. This bill would
relieve room remarketers of the need to undertake the wholesale
reprogramming of their sites to perform this task and allowing them
to meet the separate statement requirement for both New York sales
tax and New York City hotel occupancy tax with an invoice showing
such tax provided to the customer any time up to the end of the
occupancy.

Last year's bill required room remarketers to report tax in the period
in which the room remarketer debited the customer's credit card for
the occupancy. While this is the usual sales tax rule, it is not well
suited to the room remarketer industry. Because of the ease with
which reservations can be made or changed, customers of room
remarketers often cancel reservations or change the dates of the
reservations. If the reservation is made in one reporting period, and


cancelled in another, however, sales tax refund claims would be
generated, because the room remarketer would have already had to
remit to the State the sales tax due on the occupancy. This bill
would obviate the need for such refund claims by allowing room
remarketers to report the tax due on occupancy and remit the tax to
the State in the filing period in which the occupancy actually
occurs, as is current practice with respect to the New York City
hotel room occupancy tax. This bill also facilitates the process by
which room remarketers obtain credit or refund of the sales tax they
paid to the hotels that provide the occupancy that is part of the
room remarketers' transactions. Last year's bill required a room
remarketer to obtain the certificate of authority number of
the hotel that sold it the occupancy in order to qualify for a credit
or refund of the sales tax the remarketer paid the hotel for the
occupancy. Because hotels sometimes refuse to supply that number,
this bill allows room remarketers, in the event of such a refusal, to
substitute certain identifying information about the hotel, including
its address and telephone number.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
New legislation.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:
This bill would become effective on September 1, 2011, and would
apply to occupancies commencing on or after that date.
